content: Non-specific cough is characterized as a dry, non-productive cough that occurs without any identifiable respiratory disease or known underlying cause. This condition is frequently encountered in pediatric clinical practice. Children with non-specific cough are often treated with various therapies, including inhaled anticholinergic medications. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of inhaled anticholinergic medications in managing prolonged non-specific cough in children. To achieve this, comprehensive searches were conducted in databases such as the Cochrane Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE. Additionally, relevant pharmaceutical companies were contacted for information. The most recent search was performed in April 2010. The inclusion criteria required randomized controlled trials that compared inhaled anticholinergic medications with placebo treatments. However, no eligible trials meeting these criteria were identified. Consequently, no data were available for analysis. It is worth noting that a single small trial involving adults has been reported, but no such studies were found for children. The main findings of this review indicate that no randomized controlled trials have been conducted to assess the efficacy of inhaled anticholinergic medications for the treatment of prolonged non-specific cough in children. An additional search performed in April 2010 did not yield any new studies. In conclusion, there is currently no evidence to support the use of inhaled anticholinergic medications for the symptomatic management of non-specific cough in children. Further research is necessary to investigate the potential effects and benefits of this intervention in the pediatric population.
